prompt: What does an `UPDATE` do to the row it changes, in PostgreSQL?
hint: Think about what VACUUM is for.

choices.text: Overwrites the row in place, inside its page
choices.why: That is what the section says PostgreSQL never does; readers would lose the version they are entitled to.

choices.text: Writes a new version and leaves the old one behind
choices.why: Right: the old version stays until VACUUM may remove it.

choices.text: Moves the row to the end of the table and frees its old place at once
choices.why: The old place is not free until nobody can see the old version.

choices.text: Locks the whole table until it commits
choices.why: An UPDATE locks the rows it changes, not the table; and that is a different subject.

prompt: `VACUUM VERBOSE` reports `1 are dead but not yet removable` and `removable cutoff: 1098934, which was 2 XIDs old`. What is the cutoff?
hint: Who is still allowed to read the old version?

choices.text: The number of the transaction that made the dead version
choices.why: That was the UPDATE, which came after the cutoff; the cutoff belongs to the oldest snapshot.

choices.text: The last transaction VACUUM itself ran
choices.why: VACUUM does not take a transaction number for this; the cutoff comes from other sessions.

choices.text: The horizon: the oldest snapshot still in use
choices.why: Right: in the lesson it was Session A's, and nothing after it could be removed.

choices.text: How many rows the table had when VACUUM started
choices.why: That is the `remain` count on the line above.

prompt: Session A opened `REPEATABLE READ`, read the sum of prices, and sat idle while Session B raised product 7's price. What did Session A's second sum show, and why?
hint: The two totals in the transcript.

choices.text: A hundred cents more, because Session B committed
choices.why: That is what READ COMMITTED would show; REPEATABLE READ keeps its first snapshot.

choices.text: The same total, from the old row version
choices.why: Right: that is why VACUUM could not remove the old version while the transaction was open.

choices.text: An error, because the row changed under it
choices.why: A read never fails for that; a conflicting write at REPEATABLE READ is lesson 14's subject.

choices.text: It waited until Session B's transaction finished
choices.why: Readers do not wait for writers; that is what the versions are for.

prompt: Which of these hold the horizon back while they last? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them takes a new snapshot for every statement.

choices.text: An idle transaction that has updated a row
choices.why: Right: its own transaction number is in backend_xid, and every later version waits on it.

choices.text: A report query that has been running for twenty minutes
choices.why: Right: a running statement keeps its snapshot until it ends.

choices.text: An idle REPEATABLE READ transaction that has read a table
choices.why: Right: that is Session A.

choices.text: An idle READ COMMITTED transaction that has only read
choices.why: It lets go of each snapshot when its statement ends, and the finder query did not list it.

choices.text: A connection with no transaction open
choices.why: With no transaction there is no snapshot and no transaction number to hold anything.

prompt: With Session A holding the horizon, thirty seconds of the pricing robot took `products` from 5544 kB to how many megabytes?
hint: The size query after the second run.

prompt: Why was `products` almost the same size after the robot's first thirty seconds, with nothing else open?
hint: Where did the new versions go?

choices.text: The robot updated too few rows to matter
choices.why: It made 141981 updates, as many as in the second run.

choices.text: Autovacuum rewrote the table while the robot ran
choices.why: Autovacuum does not rewrite tables, and the lesson credits page tidying, not autovacuum.

choices.text: UPDATE writes in place when the price is an integer
choices.why: Every UPDATE makes a new version, whatever the type.

choices.text: Dead versions were cleared as pages filled
choices.why: Right: the horizon was free to move, so the dead versions did not pile up.

prompt: Lesson 2's tag search took 14.5 ms before and 21.1 ms while Session A was open, although it never touched Session A. What made it slower?
hint: It is a sequential scan.

choices.text: It waited for Session A's lock on `products`
choices.why: Session A only read; a read takes no lock that blocks another read.

choices.text: It read more than three times as many pages
choices.why: Right: the table grew from about 5 MB to 19 MB, and a sequential scan reads every page.

choices.text: The robot's updates changed the plan to an index scan
choices.why: There is no index that answers the tag search; lesson 8 adds one.

choices.text: The processors were busy with the robot at the same moment
choices.why: The search was timed after the robot stopped, and it stayed slow after the commit too.

prompt: After Session A committed, `VACUUM` removed all 139519 dead versions. What happened to the table's size?
hint: Where does the freed space go?

choices.text: It went back to about 5 MB
choices.why: It stayed at 19 MB; VACUUM does not hand space back except empty pages at the end.

choices.text: It stayed at 19 MB, with the space free for new versions
choices.why: Right: giving it back takes a rewrite such as VACUUM FULL, which db-administration covers.

choices.text: It doubled, because VACUUM writes a copy first
choices.why: Plain VACUUM works in place; it is VACUUM FULL that writes a new copy.

choices.text: It shrank to the size of the live rows' pages only
choices.why: The live rows are spread all over the 19 MB, so nothing at the end was empty.

prompt: A nightly job holds one `REPEATABLE READ` transaction open for three hours to export a consistent copy, while a queue table is updated all night. In the morning the queue holds 2,000 rows and its screen is slow. What is the likeliest reason?
hint: The export never reads the queue.

choices.text: The queue's rows are locked by the export
choices.why: An export only reads, and it does not lock rows against updates.

choices.text: 2,000 rows is too many for that queue screen
choices.why: 2,000 rows is small; the size of the table behind them is what grew.

choices.text: Dead versions VACUUM could not remove
choices.why: Right: the horizon is the database's, so the export held back VACUUM on a table it never read.

choices.text: Autovacuum was switched off by the export
choices.why: Autovacuum ran; it simply could not remove versions newer than the horizon.

prompt: What does `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` do when it fires?
hint: Read the severity in the transcript.

choices.text: Cancels the statement that is running
choices.why: There is no statement running; that is statement_timeout's job.

choices.text: Ends the whole session, with FATAL
choices.why: Right: the transaction is rolled back and the connection closed.

choices.text: Commits the open transaction so nothing is lost
choices.why: It never commits; committing half a transaction is what transactions exist to prevent.

choices.text: Writes a warning to the log and keeps waiting
choices.why: It acts: the session ended in the transcript.

prompt: A report runs one 40-minute `SELECT` every night and holds the horizon the whole time. Which setting would stop it?
hint: What is its state in pg_stat_activity?

choices.text: `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, set to ten minutes
choices.why: The report is active, not idle; this setting never touches it.

choices.text: `max_connections`, lowered to the number of reports
choices.why: That limits how many sessions connect, not how long one runs.

choices.text: `statement_timeout`, set for the report's role
choices.why: Right: it cancels a statement that runs too long, with an ERROR.

choices.text: `max_prepared_transactions`, set to zero
choices.why: That only concerns two-phase commit, and zero is already the default.

prompt: A checkout does `BEGIN`, updates the order, calls a payment provider that answers in two seconds, then commits. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: Which of the three shapes is it?

choices.text: Call the provider outside the transaction, before or after it
choices.why: Right: keep in the transaction only the statements that must succeed or fail together.

choices.text: Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to one second
choices.why: That would end every correct checkout halfway, with FATAL.

choices.text: Switch the transaction to REPEATABLE READ
choices.why: The level does not shorten the wait; a transaction that wrote holds the horizon at any level.

choices.text: Run VACUUM after each order
choices.why: VACUUM cannot remove what the open transactions still hold.

prompt: To give every new session on `market` a one-minute limit on idle transactions, you run `ALTER ___ market SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '1min';`.
hint: The setting is attached to an object, not to a session.

prompt: A team sets `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '2s'` for the whole server after an incident. What is the first thing likely to break?
hint: Who has legitimate idle gaps longer than that?

choices.text: Nothing; correct code is never idle for two seconds
choices.why: A correct transaction can wait on a person, a slow network or a migration step.

choices.text: Every running query longer than two seconds
choices.why: Running queries are active, not idle; this setting does not touch them.

choices.text: Autovacuum, which cannot run with a timeout set
choices.why: Autovacuum is not an idle client transaction.

choices.text: Correct transactions with longer pauses, ended with FATAL
choices.why: Right: the value has to sit above the longest idle gap a correct transaction has.

prompt: Why does `oldest.sql` sort by the age in transactions rather than by how long the transaction has been open?
hint: What makes a held horizon expensive?

choices.text: Because `xact_start` is empty for idle sessions
choices.why: It is filled for any open transaction; the finder printed open_for from it.

choices.text: It follows the writes, and so the damage
choices.why: Right: an old transaction on an idle server costs little; a young one on a busy server costs a lot.

choices.text: Because the clock on a server is not reliable
choices.why: The clock is fine; it just measures time, not dead versions.

choices.text: Because age() is faster to compute
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; both are trivial.

prompt: In the finder's output, one row has a number under `xid` and nothing under `xmin`. What kind of session is it?
hint: A transaction only gets a number of its own when it does one thing.

choices.text: A REPEATABLE READ transaction that has only read
choices.why: That one had a snapshot (xmin) and no number of its own.

choices.text: A statement that is still running
choices.why: A running statement has a snapshot, so xmin is filled.

choices.text: An idle transaction that has written something
choices.why: Right: the UPDATE gave it a transaction number, and idle it holds no snapshot.

choices.text: A connection outside any transaction
choices.why: With no transaction it would have neither column, and the finder would not list it.

prompt: `~/oldest.sql` returns no rows, and yet `VACUUM VERBOSE` still reports a cutoff millions of transactions old. Where do you look next?
hint: Some holders have no row in pg_stat_activity.

choices.text: `pg_stat_user_tables`, for the dead rows
choices.why: That shows the symptom, not who is holding the horizon.

choices.text: `pg_locks`, for a lock on the table
choices.why: A lock does not hold the horizon; a transaction or a slot does.

choices.text: The server log, for the last checkpoint
choices.why: Checkpoints have nothing to do with which versions VACUUM may remove.

choices.text: `pg_prepared_xacts` and `pg_replication_slots`
choices.why: Right: a forgotten prepared transaction or a slot nobody reads holds the horizon with no session.

prompt: Match each holder of the horizon to the setting or action that ends it.
hint: Two of them are timeouts, and two are not sessions at all.

pairs.left: a session idle in a transaction
a statement running for an hour

prompt: In the finder's output, how many transactions old were the three sessions holding the horizon?
hint: The xid_age column.

prompt: Put the experiment of the bloat section in the order it was run.
hint: The baseline comes before anything is held.
items: Measure the table's size and the tag search
Run the robot with nothing else open
Open Session A and leave it idle
Run the robot again for the same thirty seconds
Commit Session A and run VACUUM
trap: Without the first run, there is nothing to compare the held run against; without the commit, VACUUM cannot remove anything.

prompt: A monitoring alert fires when any session has been `idle in transaction` for more than five minutes. A developer's `psql` sat in `BEGIN` all weekend on a server that received no writes, and the alert fired. How much bloat did that transaction cause?
hint: Dead versions come from writes.

choices.text: A weekend's worth, in every table of the database
choices.why: Without writes there were no dead versions to keep; the clock alone makes none.

choices.text: Almost none: nothing was written
choices.why: Right: which is why the lesson alerts on age in transactions rather than on time alone.

choices.text: Exactly the size of the tables it read
choices.why: Reading makes no copies at all.

choices.text: It cannot be known until VACUUM FULL is run
choices.why: VACUUM VERBOSE and n_dead_tup answer it without rewriting anything.

prompt: Which is the correct order of fixes when `oldest.sql` lists a writer, a REPEATABLE READ reader and a running report, all of the same age?
hint: One of them holds something besides the horizon.

choices.text: The report first, because it is active
choices.why: Being active is not what makes it urgent; the writer also holds locks.

choices.text: The writer first, then look again
choices.why: Right: and the next oldest becomes the horizon as soon as the first goes.

choices.text: All three at once with a server restart
choices.why: A restart ends everybody's work to end three transactions.

choices.text: None, because VACUUM will catch up on its own
choices.why: VACUUM cannot pass the horizon however often it runs.
